steps.scene: You're waiting to pull out of a side road. Parked vans line the main road on your right. You look, and the road reads clear.

question.prompt: Why look again before you go?

options.text: A motorcycle is easily hidden behind an obstruction
Once it looked clear, it's clear — go before it changes
Motorcycles have priority over cars emerging

question.explanation: A bike is narrow enough to sit entirely behind a parked van. Look again, and look for the small shape.

steps.scene: You're easing up to a junction on a bend. The thick pillar between your windscreen and side window sweeps across your view.

options.text: The pillar is too narrow to hide anything that matters
Pillars only block your view on fast, open roads
Move your head to look around it before you commit

question.explanation: At bends and junctions a windscreen pillar can hide a whole rider, cyclist or pedestrian. Lean and look past it.

steps.title: Where bikes go missing
steps.body: Junctions are where motorcyclists and cyclists are hardest to see: small, often masked by traffic, and arriving faster than you expect.

question.prompt: Where are you most likely to miss a motorcyclist or cyclist?

options.text: On dual carriageways
At junctions
Anywhere — a car is the thing you're really looking for

question.explanation: Bikes are the road users drivers most often miss at junctions. Make looking for them a separate, deliberate check.

steps.title: The check just before you turn right
steps.body: Waiting to turn right into a side road, take a last look in the right mirror and blind spot. Something may be overtaking the queue you're in.

question.prompt: What are you looking for in that final right-mirror check?

options.text: Traffic overtaking you on your right
Nothing — your indicator has already warned them
Whether the side road you're entering is clear

question.explanation: A rider may never have seen your signal, and the road behind changed while you waited. Look before you turn across it.

steps.scene: Traffic is crawling in two lanes. A gap opens in the lane beside you and you're about to move across into it.

options.text: Nothing can be moving between lanes in a slow queue
Mirrors and blind spot, for a rider filtering past
Sound the horn and flash to claim the gap

question.explanation: In queues, motorcyclists filter past on either side. Mirror and blind-spot check every time you change lane.

steps.title: Reading a rider's shoulder check
steps.body: A rider glancing back over their right shoulder is checking their blind area. It usually means they're about to change direction.

question.prompt: The rider ahead glances over their right shoulder just before a right turn. Why?

options.text: To help them balance through the turn
To check for traffic in their blind area
Motorcycles aren't fitted with mirrors

question.explanation: Spot that glance and you know what's coming next. Hold back rather than drawing alongside.

steps.wrongBelief: A bike with its headlight on in daylight is impossible to miss.

question.prompt: A motorbike comes towards you in bright sunshine with its headlight on. Why?

options.text: So you can see the rider more easily
The rider is inviting you to go first
To help the rider see further ahead

question.explanation: The light helps them stand out, but a bike is still narrow and easily lost behind other traffic.

steps.repairNote: Headlights and bright kit make a rider easier to see — they don't make one impossible to miss. Look for the bike itself.
